'''''Cucumis metuliferus''''',  also known as the '''African horned cucumber''' (shortened to '''horned cucumber'''), '''horned melon''', '''spiked melon''', '''jelly melon''', or '''kiwano''', is an annual [[vine]] in the [[cucumber]] and melon family [[Cucurbitaceae]]. Its fruit has [[horn (anatomy)|horn]]-like [[spine (botany)|spines]], hence the name "horned melon". The ripe fruit has orange skin and lime-green, soft flesh. ''Cucumis metuliferus'' is native to [[Southern Africa]],<ref>{{cite web |last1=Welman |first1=Mienkie |title=Cucumis metuliferus |url=http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantcd/cucumismet.htm |website=PlantZAfrica.com |publisher=South African National Biodiversity Institute |access-date=7 June 2015 |archive-date=10 May 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510134015/http://www.plantzafrica.com/plantcd/cucumismet.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name="seattletimes" /> in [[South Africa]], [[Namibia]], [[Botswana]], [[Zambia]], [[Malawi]], [[Zimbabwe]], [[Mozambique]], and [[Angola]].

== Consumption and other uses ==
Kiwano is a traditional food plant in Africa. Along with the gemsbok cucumber (''[[Acanthosicyos naudinianus]]'') and ''tsamma'' ([[citron melon]]), it is one of the few sources of water during the dry season in the [[Kalahari Desert]].<ref name="setvkhalagadi">{{in lang|fr}} ''Parc de Khal-agadi, pas si désert'', in [[Science & Vie]] n° 1130, November 2011, pp. 18–21.</ref><ref>{{cite book |author=Ben-Erik Van Wyk |date=2000 |title=People's Plants: A guide to useful plants of southern Africa |url=http://www.briza.co.za/catalog/product_info.php?products_id=124 |location=South Africa |publisher=Briza Publications |page=38 |isbn=978-1-875093-19-9 |access-date=10 January 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150626102929/http://www.briza.co.za/catalog/product_info.php?products_id=124 |archive-date=26 June 2015 |url-status=dead}}</ref> In northern Zimbabwe, it is called ''gaka'' or ''gakachika'',<ref>{{Cite book |title=Edible Medicinal And Non-Medicinal Plants: Volume 2, Fruits |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6fJyQDil1rYC&pg=PA235 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |date=30 January 2012 |isbn=9789400717633 |language=en |first=T. K. |last=Lim}}</ref> and is primarily used as a snack or salad, and rarely for decoration. It can be eaten at any stage of ripening.

''C. metuliferus'' may be used as a [[rootstock]] (via grafting) for melon to prevent both growth reduction and a strong [[nematode]] buildup in ''M. incognita''-infested soil.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Sigüenza |first1=Concepcion |last2=Schochow |first2=Martin |last3=Turini |first3=Tom |last4=Ploeg |first4=Antoon |title=Use of Cucumis metuliferus as a Rootstock for Melon to Manage Meloidogyne incognita |journal=Journal of Nematology |date=2005 |volume=37 |issue=3 |pages=276–280 |issn=0022-300X |pmc=2620981 |pmid=19262873}}</ref>

The fruit's taste has been compared to a combination of banana and [[passionfruit]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://enzedexotics.com/2019/03/25/what-does-kiwano-taste-like/ |title=What does kiwano taste like?}}</ref> cucumber and zucchini<ref name="seattletimes">{{cite web |url=https://archive.seattletimes.com/archive/20060222/hornedmelon22/kiwano-its-whats-inside-that-counts |title=Living - Kiwano: It's what's inside that counts - Seattle Times Newspaper |work=nwsource.com}}</ref> or a combination of banana, cucumber and [[Lime (fruit)|lime]].<ref>{{cite web |url=http://deseretnews.com/article/1,5143,695254222,00.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080226181024/http://deseretnews.com/article/1,5143,695254222,00.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=26 February 2008 |title=The Dinner Diva: Let's discover some more little-known fruits |date=21 February 2008 |work=DeseretNews.com}}</ref> 

Some also eat the peel, which is very rich in [[vitamin C|vitamin'' ''C]] and [[dietary fiber]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Mountain Herb Estate - VEGETABLE - CUCUMBER, AFRICAN HORNED, Jelly Melon, Kiwano, Rooi-agurkie, Rooikomkommer (Afr.), Mokapana (Tswana) (Cucumis metuliferus) |url=http://www.herbgarden.co.za/mountainherb/herbinfo.php?id=366 |website=www.herbgarden.co.za |access-date=7 June 2015}}</ref>

==Germination==
[[Germination]] is optimal between {{cvt|20-35|C}}; is delayed at {{cvt|12|C}} and [[Stratification_(seeds)|seed stratification]] is totally inhibited; and is greatly inhibited above {{cvt|35|C}}. [[Salinity]] increases the time required for full germination. The [[sowing]] dates greatly influence fruit yield and [[flowering]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benzioni |first1=A. |last2=Mendlinger |first2=S. |last3=Ventura |first3=M. |last4=Huyskens |first4=S. |date=Aug 1991 |title=Effect of Sowing Dates, Temperatures on Germination, Flowering, and Yield of ''Cucumis metuliferus'' |url=https://journals.ashs.org/hortsci/view/journals/hortsci/26/8/article-p1051.xml |journal=[[HortScience]] |volume=26 |issue=8 |pages=1051–1053 |doi=10.21273/HORTSCI.26.8.1051 |issn=0018-5345 |publisher=[[American Society for Horticultural Science]] |access-date=29 May 2025}}</ref>

==Pests and diseases==
Kiwano is resistant to several [[root-knot nematodes]]; two [[Accession_number_(bioinformatics)|accessions]] were found to be highly resistant to [[watermelon mosaic virus]], but very sensitive to the [[squash mosaic virus]]. Some accessions were found to succumb to [[Fusarium wilt|''Fusarium'' wilt]]. Resistance to [[greenhouse whitefly]] was reported. Kiwano was reported to be resistant to [[powdery mildew]], but in Israel, powdery mildew and squash mosaic virus attacked kiwano fields and control measures had to be taken.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Benzioni |first1=Aliza |title=Kiwano - New Crop FactSHEET |url=http://www.hort.purdue.edu/newcrop/cropfactsheets/kiwano.html |website=Center for New Crops & Plant Products |publisher=[[Purdue University]] |access-date=3 June 2015 |date=1997 |location=West Lafayette, IN}}</ref>

== Fruit development ==
During 28 days of development on the plant, fresh weight, [[Electrical resistivity and conductivity|electrical conductivity]] and [[Titratable_acid|titratable acidity]] of fruits do not change, [[pH]] rises and then falls, and concentrations of [[Reducing sugar|reducing sugars]] and [[total soluble solids]] increase. In the same period, [[Peel_(fruit)|peel]] colour changes from green through whitish green to yellow and finally to orange, and the [[pigment]] profile shows a decline in pigments absorbing at 431 and 663'' ''nm, and a rapid increase in those absorbing at 442 and 470'' ''nm.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mendlinger |first1=S. |last2=Benzioni |first2=A. |last3=Huyskens |first3=S. |last4=Ventura |first4=M. |title=Fruit development and postharvest physiology of ''Cucumis metuliferus'' Mey., a new crop plant |url=http://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/00221589.1992.11516274 |journal=Journal of Horticultural Science |date=1992 |volume=67 |issue=4 |pages=489–493 |doi=10.1080/00221589.1992.11516274 |issn=0022-1589 |access-date=26 August 2024 |url-access=subscription |publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]]}}</ref>
